entities.name: Philo of Larissa
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Philo of Larissa (c. 154/153 – 83 BCE) served as the eleventh and final scholarch of Plato's Academy in Athens, succeeding Clitomachus around 110 BCE. As the head of this venerable institution, Philo became a pivotal figure in the evolution of Academic Skepticism, a dominant philosophical school of the Hellenistic period. His tenure marked a critical juncture, as he sought to reconcile the radical Pyrrhonist-influenced skepticism of his predecessors, Arcesilaus and Carneades, with a more nuanced interpretation of Platonic thought, thereby laying groundwork for a potential return to dogmatism.

Philo's philosophical career was characterized by his attempt to clarify and moderate the Academic position on the possibility of knowledge. He argued that while certain knowledge (catalepsis) of things in themselves was unattainable, there existed a 'non-evident' apprehension (acatalepsia) that allowed for reasonable belief and action in daily life. This distinction was central to his 'Fourth Academy,' which departed from the more extreme suspension of judgment advocated by Carneades. Following the outbreak of the First Mithridatic War in 88 BCE, Philo, along with many other Athenian intellectuals, fled to Rome, where he established a school and taught prominent Roman aristocrats, including Cicero, profoundly influencing the latter's philosophical development.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Philo of Larissa significantly influenced the transmission of Greek philosophy to Rome, particularly Academic Skepticism, directly shaping the thought of figures like Cicero. His nuanced reinterpretation of skepticism marked the end of a major philosophical tradition and paved the way for new forms of Platonism.
